title: Hornbill: We're Not Afraid to Die... if We Can All Be Together

learn.hook: A family of four leaves England to sail around the world, retracing a voyage made two centuries earlier. What could go wrong? Almost everything.
points: A true survival account written by Gordon Cook and Alan East, narrated in the first person by the father, who is the ship's captain.
The text falls into three sections: the voyage and the first great wave; the fight to keep afloat; the search for and sighting of the island.
In July 1976 the narrator, his wife Mary, son Jonathan (6) and daughter Suzanne (7) set sail from Plymouth, England.
Their aim: to repeat the round-the-world voyage made 200 years earlier by Captain James Cook.
Their boat, Wavewalker, was a 23-metre, 30-ton wooden-hulled ship, professionally built, fitted out over months and tested in rough weather.

steps: Start: July 1976.

example.answer: July 1976, Plymouth; retrace Captain Cook's voyage; aboard the 23-metre, 30-ton Wavewalker.

learn.reallife: Indian Navy officers Dilip Donde and Abhilash Tomy sailed solo around the world, and the INSV Tarini crew of women officers did it too. Long voyages need the same careful preparation as Wavewalker.

topics.title: Into the southern Indian Ocean: precautions

learn.hook: When waves start rising like mountains, a good captain doesn't panic. He runs a checklist. This section is that checklist.
points: At Cape Town two crewmen joined them, American Larry Vigil and Swiss Herb Seigler, to help on one of the world's roughest seas, the southern Indian Ocean.
They celebrated Christmas about 3,500 km east of Cape Town, despite the bad weather.
On 2 January the waves grew gigantic and the wind howled.
Precautions: they slowed the ship by dropping the storm jib, lashed a heavy mooring rope in a loop across the stern, and double-lashed everything on deck.
They went through their life-raft drill, attached life-lines, and put on oilskins and life jackets.

example.q: List the steps the captain took to protect Wavewalker from the storm.
steps: Slow the ship: drop the storm jib.
Steady her: lash a heavy mooring rope in a loop across the stern.
Secure everything: double-lash all items; practise the life-raft drill.
Protect people: life-lines, oilskins and life jackets.
example.answer: He dropped the storm jib, looped a mooring rope across the stern, double-lashed everything, ran the life-raft drill and had everyone wear life-lines, oilskins and life jackets.

learn.reallife: Before a cyclone, Indian fishermen in Odisha and Andhra pull boats ashore and tie them down, following IMD warnings. Preparation saves lives, as on Wavewalker.

topics.title: The great wave and the flooded ship

learn.hook: One wave, almost twice the height of the others, picks up a 30-ton ship. The captain is thrown into the sea, and only a life-line pulls him back.
points: On 2 January an enormous wave struck; the narrator's head hit the wheel and he was swept overboard.
The ship righted itself; his life-line jerked tight and he grabbed the guard rails and got back on board.
His injuries: cracked ribs and a mouth full of blood and broken teeth. Mary took the wheel and held the ship steady.
Water poured in through a broken hatch and a gaping hole; the ship was listing and taking in water fast.
Larry and Herb pumped for hours; the narrator stretched canvas and fixed waterproof hatch covers across the holes, so most water was deflected over the side.

example.q: How did the narrator stop water from pouring in?
steps: Find what is broken: the hatch and a gaping hole.
Cover the gaps with canvas and waterproof hatch covers.
Result: most water now ran off over the side.
example.answer: He stretched canvas and fixed waterproof hatch covers over the gaps, so most water was deflected over the side.

learn.reallife: Coast Guard and NDRF teams in Kerala's 2018 floods also worked on two fronts at once: stop water coming in, and get water out. The Wavewalker crew did both.

topics.title: Pumps, a brave daughter and a tiny island

learn.hook: When your seven-year-old hides a head injury so as not to distract you, and your six-year-old says he's not afraid to die if the family is together, you fight harder.
points: Problems: the hand pumps blocked with debris and the electric pump short-circuited.
Solution: the narrator found another electric pump, connected it to an outlet pipe, and it worked.
Sue had a huge bump on her head, two black eyes and a deep cut on her arm, but did not complain because she did not want to worry her father.
Jonathan told his father that they were not afraid of dying if they could all be together, which gave the title.
With little equipment, the narrator worked out their position and set a course for Ile Amsterdam, a tiny island, a pinprick in the vast ocean.

learn.hook: After days of pumping, a kid's hand-drawn card and a hug decide the mood on board. Then two small voices shout that they can see land.
points: 4 January: after about 36 hours of pumping, the water was under control; they ate their first proper meal in almost two days, and felt relieved.
The relief was short-lived: the wind rose again, and by 5 January the situation was desperate.
Sue gave her parents a card with caricatures of them, telling them how much she loved them and thanking them.
Jonathan hugged his father and called him the best daddy and the best captain in the world.
On 6 January, in the evening, the children spotted Ile Amsterdam; the people at the island's French scientific base helped them ashore.

example.q: Board question: Describe the mental condition of the voyagers on 4 and 5 January.
steps: 4 January: pumping succeeded; they ate and felt relief and hope.
Then the wind returned.
5 January: the situation was desperate; they feared for their lives but kept spirits up.
example.answer: On 4 January they felt relief and hope; on 5 January they were full of fear and near despair, yet the children's love kept them going.

learn.reallife: The Indian Coast Guard and Navy run search-and-rescue across a huge area of the Indian Ocean. A sighting of land or a rescue ship after days at sea still brings the same 'Land ho!' joy.

learn.hook: Adults panic about what could happen; children trust whoever is in charge. In this crisis, the kids end up as the steadiest people on board.
points: The narrator: calm, resourceful and determined captain; also a loving father who feels responsible for everyone.
Mary: brave and steady; she held the wheel through the most crucial hours and supported the family.
Larry and Herb: tireless crewmen who pumped for hours and never gave up.
Sue and Jonathan: show remarkable maturity, courage and optimism; adults feel fear more openly, children show trust and love.

Narration shifts: Section 1 – an adventurous voyage turning into crisis; Section 2 – desperate struggle to survive; Section 3 – hope, relief and rescue. Possible subtitles: 'The Voyage Begins', 'Fighting to Stay Afloat', 'Land Ho!'

learn.hook: Why would anyone choose to sail into the world's roughest ocean? And what do you learn when you almost don't come back?
points: Courage and optimism: the family keeps hope alive under extreme stress.
Teamwork, family bonding and leadership: everyone has a job, and the captain leads calmly.
Human endurance against nature's fury: the ocean is huge and powerful, but persistence wins.
Why people take hazardous voyages: the thrill of adventure, testing one's limits, discovery, and a chance to see life's essentials clearly.
Lessons from facing death: love, unity and optimism matter most; panic helps no one.

example.q: Discussion: What lessons can one learn from facing death in this account?
steps: Optimism kept them working even when things looked hopeless.

example.answer: Hope, unity and calm thinking matter most when life is at stake.

learn.reallife: Mountaineers like Bachendri Pal and Arunima Sinha talk about the same reasons for risky journeys: testing oneself, and coming back with a clearer view of life.

topics.title: Sea words: from stern to starboard

learn.hook: Stern, jib, hatch, starboard: if sailing words sound like a foreign language, this topic is your phrasebook.
points: Expressions: 'honing our seafaring skills' = sharpening sailing skills; 'ominous silence' = a threatening quiet; 'Mayday calls' = international radio distress calls; 'pinpricks in the vast ocean' = tiny islands; 'a tousled head' = messy, untidy hair.

Ship parts: bow = front; stern = back; port = left side and starboard = right side (facing forward); deck = floor on top; hull = body of the ship; hatch = opening in the deck; jib = triangular front sail.

Everyday meanings: knot (unit of ship speed / a tied loop), stern (strict / back of a ship), boom (sudden growth / sail pole), hatch (to come out of an egg / deck opening), anchor (TV presenter / weight that holds a ship).
Ship compounds: airship (powered balloon), flagship (lead ship, or best product of a company), lightship (anchored ship with a light that works as a lighthouse).
'Take on': here 'take on water' = let water in; also take on staff (employ), take on a job (accept), take on a rival (compete with).

example.q: What does 'take on' mean in: (a) The ship took on water. (b) The firm took on ten engineers.
steps: (a) Water came into the ship.
(b) The firm employed them.

learn.hook: The English word 'catamaran' sailed in from Tamil. Indian boat words and boatmen's songs are part of the same story of the sea.
points: 'Catamaran' comes from Tamil 'kattumaram', meaning 'tied wood': logs tied together to make a boat.
Indian languages have many words for storm, such as toofan and aandhi in Hindi; and many vessel names such as dhow, dinghy, kayak, canoe, junk and catamaran.
India has rich boatmen's songs, like the bhatiyali of Bengal and the vanchipattu of Kerala.

Body 3: teamwork keeps the ship afloat; they reach Ile Amsterdam.
Conclusion: hope turned despair into survival.
example.answer: A structured answer: intro, three evidence-based points, conclusion linking optimism to survival.

learn.reallife: Kerala's snake-boat races during Onam are accompanied by vanchipattu boat songs. Every coast has its own sea vocabulary and music.

quiz.q: 'Catamaran' comes from which language?
quiz.explain: It comes from Tamil 'kattumaram', meaning tied wood.
quiz.mistake: Assumes a European origin for a sea word

quiz.q: What does 'kattumaram' literally mean?
quiz.explain: The boat was made of logs tied together.
quiz.mistake: Guesses from use rather than origin

quiz.q: Which is a boatmen's song tradition from Bengal?
quiz.explain: Bhatiyali songs were sung by boatmen on Bengal's rivers.

quiz.q: Which word is a Hindi word for a storm?
quiz.explain: Toofan means storm; naav means boat, lehar means wave, kinara means shore.

quiz.q: Which question suits a long answer best?
options: How did optimism help them survive?
Where did Larry join the ship?
How old was Jonathan on the trip?
quiz.explain: It needs discussion with several points; the others are one-line facts.
quiz.mistake: Thinks factual recall needs long answers

quiz.q: Extract: Sue said she did not want to worry her father. This shows she was:
quiz.explain: She put her parents' peace of mind above her own pain.

quiz.q: In a short answer on the pumps, which detail is essential?
options: The exact ages of the children
The spare electric pump that worked
quiz.explain: The key fact is the spare pump that finally worked.

quiz.q: Which is the best title-based answer: 'Why is the account called We're Not Afraid to Die...'?

It is the name of the island
It is the motto of Captain Cook

quiz.mistake: Links the title to a place or object
